sentences.text: For more than a thousand years, nothing could break the walls of Constantinople.
Arab armies tried, twice.
Fleets tried.
Even a Crusader army managed to get in, in twelve oh four, though that one hardly counts, since it was supposedly on the city's side.
Then, in the spring of fourteen fifty-three, a twenty-one-year-old sultan parked his army outside them.
In just under eight weeks, the Roman Empire was over.
Here's the thing.
Ask historians what actually broke those walls, and you won't get an answer.
You'll get an argument.
Some will blame a cannon.
Some will blame a small door that somebody forgot to lock.
And some will blame one wounded man, carried off the wall at exactly the wrong moment.
Three suspects.
One city.
And a set of witnesses that includes a Venetian who disliked the Genoese, a Genoese archbishop who disliked the Venetians, and a Greek chronicler with firm opinions about almost everyone.
So we'll go carefully.
By the end, I'll tell you which suspect I would arrest.
Or, and this is the uncomfortable possibility, why the question itself may be slightly wrong.
But first, the scene.
It is the evening of the twenty-eighth of May, fourteen fifty-three.
The emperor is riding to Hagia Sophia, the Great Church, to make his peace with God.
Beyond the walls, the Ottoman camp glows like a second city.
Inside, fewer than seven thousand men are waiting for something like eighty thousand to come at them.
Hold that picture.
We'll come back to it.
But to understand how it came to this, we need to meet the man on that road, and the empire he inherited, which by then fit comfortably inside a single set of walls.
His name was Constantine Palaiologos.
Constantine the Eleventh, if you're counting, and the Byzantines were.
He was born in fourteen oh four, the fourth son of an emperor, which is not a position that comes with high expectations.
His brother John, the emperor, died without an heir in October fourteen forty-eight.
In January fourteen forty-nine, Constantine was proclaimed emperor in a small ceremony in the Peloponnese.
He was never crowned in Hagia Sophia, as custom required.
Which tells you roughly how the empire was doing.
And what, exactly, was he emperor of?
By fourteen-fifty, the Romans, and yes, they still called themselves Romans, held one city, a few islands, and the southern Peloponnese.
The great capital had been captured once before, in twelve oh four, by Crusaders, and it had never really recovered.
Constantine had no children, and every attempt to find a wife, in Aragon, in Georgia, in Trebizond, fell through.
An emperor with no heir, no wife, and not much of an empire.
But he did have the walls.
So let's talk about those walls, because everything that follows hangs on them.
On the land side, they ran for about four miles, and they came in layers.
First a ditch, around sixty feet wide.
Then a low outer wall, some twenty-five feet high.
Then, behind it, a taller inner wall, forty feet or more, studded with towers.
An attacker had to cross all of it, under fire.
They had been standing since the fifth century.
There was only one soft spot, a dip in the ground where a little river valley, the Lycus, cut through the line.
The Greeks called it the Mesoteichion, the middle wall.
Remember that name.
Now, the walls were one problem.
The other was the Pope.
Rome would send help, but only if the Greek Church formally accepted union with the Catholic Church.
On the twelfth of December, fourteen fifty-two, that union was proclaimed in Hagia Sophia itself.
A great many people hated it.
A monk named Gennadius warned that the city would be lost and its people sold into slavery, and a riot followed.
One chronicler says plenty of people accepted the union only because they planned to quietly undo it once the Turks went home.
Nothing brings a besieged city together like a theological argument, in the sense that everyone is furious at the same time.
So that's the defender: a thin empire, a divided church, a very good wall, and almost nobody to stand on it.
Now meet the man who was coming to knock, and the most expensive job application in medieval history, which was sent to the wrong address.
Mehmed the Second was born on the thirtieth of March, fourteen thirty-two, the son of a sultan and a mother who had been a slave.
He was handed the throne at twelve, when his father, Murad, stepped down.
It lasted about two years.
Hungary broke a truce, the advisers panicked, and Murad came back to lead the army.
The boy sultan was sent off to govern a province instead.
Imagine being a sultan at twelve and being retired by fourteen.
It does something to a person.
In Mehmed's case, it seems to have produced a very particular kind of determination.
His father died in February fourteen fifty-one, and Mehmed took the throne again, at nineteen.
Later writers say that one of his first acts was to have his infant half-brother drowned.
The historian Edwin Pears warns that both Turkish and Christian writers are unreliable on Mehmed, so take that detail with a pinch of salt.
What isn't in doubt is the voice at his elbow.
A scholar named Akshamsaddin had been telling him since boyhood that Constantinople was his to take.
The emperor, for his part, made an early and expensive mistake.
Back in fourteen fifty-one, the Ottomans were paying the Byzantines to keep a rival claimant to the throne, a prince named Orhan, safely in Constantinople.
Constantine's envoys now asked for the allowance to be doubled, and hinted that Orhan might otherwise be let go.
It was a bluff.
Mehmed didn't blink, and he now had a perfect excuse for war.
Two years later, Orhan tried to escape the fallen city dressed as a Greek monk.
Another prisoner betrayed him, and he was beheaded on the spot.
In the spring of fourteen fifty-two, he showed everyone what he meant.
At the narrowest point of the Bosphorus, about six hundred and sixty meters across, he began to build a fortress.
Right on the European shore, which was Byzantine territory, in defiance of the treaties.
He supervised the work himself.
The emperor's envoys protested; Mehmed fobbed them off.
By the end of August it was finished, and the Turks gave it a name: Boghaz-kesen.
The Cutter of the Strait.
Or, depending on how you translate it, the Cutter of the Throat.
Subtle, he was not.
That November, a Venetian ship ignored the signal to stop.
The fortress's guns brought it down.
The captain, a man named Rizzo, was impaled and left by the roadside, and his crew were beheaded.
Until then, many in the West had hoped the young sultan was bluffing.
That was the end of the hope.
Fortresses and fleets are one thing.
Walls like Constantinople's are another.
For those, Mehmed needed something bigger, and here's the irony: he got it from the emperor's own doorstep.
Sometime around fourteen fifty-two, a cannon-founder named Urban turned up in Constantinople.
Hungarian, say some sources.
Wallachian, say others.
Everyone agrees he was excellent at casting bronze guns, and rather unlucky at being paid.
He offered his services to the emperor.
Constantine could not afford his salary, and could not even supply the metal.
So Urban left, and went to see the sultan.
Mehmed questioned him closely.
Could he make a gun that would break the walls of Constantinople?
Urban said he could make one that would blast the walls of Babylon.
He was given four times the salary he'd asked of the emperor.
Which is a lesson in recruitment, if nothing else.
Now, to be fair, Mehmed had plenty of other cannon.
But the monster, the one the chroniclers kept coming back to, began life as an unpaid bill.
It was hauled toward the city that winter by sixty oxen, with two hundred men walking alongside to steady it and another two hundred ahead, preparing the road.
By the end of March, it was within five miles of the walls.
How big was it?
Honestly, nobody agrees.
The sources give a stone ball weighing hundreds of kilos, somewhere between roughly two hundred and seventy and five hundred and fifty, depending on whom you trust.
What they do agree on is how often it could fire.
Seven times a day.
That's all.
The gun needed so much tending that it could barely manage a handful of shots before the sun went down.
Seven shots a day.
Remember that number.
It matters later.
Meanwhile, inside the city, the emperor wanted to know exactly how many men he had.
He asked his adviser, George Sphrantzes, to count every man who could carry a weapon.
Sphrantzes did the sums and brought back the total.
The emperor, we're told, wanted it kept secret.
In a moment, you'll see why.
